title: Okoho Soup
author: Ene Ochigbo
desc: A stem peeled into thin strands, soaked fifteen minutes in hot water and squeezed until the water runs thick — that sap is the thickener, and nothing else in Nigeria works this way.
longDesc: Okoho is the Idoma soup of Benue and it is the most unusual preparation in this entire collection. The thickener is not a seed or a flour but the sap of a plant stem: the okoho stick is peeled into thin strands, soaked in hot water for fifteen minutes, and then squeezed until the liquid is very thick and slippery. Egusi balls are dropped into the broth and steamed firm, everything is lifted out while the okoho sap simmers ten minutes on low, and then it all goes back in. Two varieties of locust bean, dawadawa and iru, are used together.
ingredients: 1 medium stick or stem of okoho plant
Hot water, for soaking the strands
Dried fish, medium size, preferably dried catfish
Locust beans — 2 balls of 2 varieties, dawadawa and iru
1/4 kilo of beef, or dried bush meat
steps: Wash and peel the okoho stem into thin strands, and soak them in hot water for 15 minutes.
Squeeze the sap from the strands until the liquid is very thick, and reserve it.
Parboil the beef or dried meat with the onions, salt and ground pepper.
Add the ground locust beans and the dried fish, and cook 15 minutes.
Blend the egusi until smooth, add the crayfish, and mix with minimal water until the oil forms.
Drop small egusi balls into the boiling broth and cover to steam until firm.
Remove the meat, the egusi balls and the fish from the pot.
Add the okoho sap and simmer on low heat 10 minutes.
Return the meat, egusi and fish, stir briefly, and serve.
chefTips: Thick and slippery is the squeeze endpoint. Keep working the strands in the water until the liquid visibly changes — that is the whole dish.
Beat the stem gently with a pestle first to loosen the bark, then strip the rope-like inner layer and discard the woody stick. The inner layer is what holds the sap.
Take everything out before the sap goes in. The sap needs ten minutes on low heat undisturbed and the solids get in the way.
Low heat for the sap. Hard boiling will break the mucilage down and you lose the thickening.
Two varieties of locust bean, dawadawa and iru, used together. No other recipe in this collection does that.
Firm to the touch is the cue for the egusi balls. Steam them covered and do not stir.
The hot-water soak is given as fifteen minutes here and as eight to ten minutes by another named source. Both then squeeze, and the endpoint is the same.
commonMistakes: Boiling the sap hard, which destroys the thickening.
Leaving the meat and egusi in while the sap simmers.
Stopping the squeeze before the liquid goes thick and slippery.
Keeping the woody stick in rather than stripping the inner layer.
Stirring the egusi balls before they are firm.
sources: Adapted from 'OKOHO SOUP (An Idoma Delicacy)', Nigeria Galleria — no author provided on the page, credited to the publisher. Headnote as printed: 'An Idoma Delicacy'.

Quantities exactly as printed: 1 medium size stick or stem of Okoho plant; Dried fish (medium size) preferably dried cat fish; Seeds of fresh pepper (Tarodo); Locust beans 2 balls of 2 varieties (dawadawa and iru); Egusi (one cup); Onions (one medium size); A pinch of crayfish; 2 maggi cubes for seasoning; 1/4 kilo of beef or dried bush meat; Salt. NOTE: the dried fish, the pepper seeds and the salt carry no quantities. Yield not specified.

Method and times as printed: wash and peel the okoho stem into thin strands and soak in hot water 15 minutes; squeeze the sap from the strands until very thick and reserve the liquid; parboil the beef or dried meat with onions, salt and ground pepper; add the ground locust beans and dried fish and cook 15 minutes; blend the egusi until smooth, add crayfish, mix with minimal water until oil forms; drop small egusi balls into the boiling broth and cover to steam until firm; remove the meat, egusi balls and fish; add the okoho sap and simmer on low heat 10 minutes; return the meat, egusi and fish and stir briefly.
DONENESS CUES as printed: egusi balls 'firm to touch'; the okoho sap simmers about 10 minutes.

THE BETTER EXTRACTION DESCRIPTION comes from the second named source and is used in the tips above: 'The Idoma's Special Delicacy: Okoho Soup', byline Omakeche Rebecca Odoh, iambenue.com. Her method for the stalk: peel the bark by scratching gently with a knife; place on a clean surface and hit gently with a pestle to loosen; remove the rope-like layer and discard the stick; wrap the layer, place in a bowl, add hot water, let sit 8 to 10 minutes; squeeze in the bowl 'until the water becomes thick and slippery'. THAT SQUEEZE ENDPOINT is the real doneness cue for the extraction and it is better than anything in the first source. Her article gives NO QUANTITIES and states so.
LOCAL NAMES ACROSS LANGUAGES, from Odoh: Okoho (Idoma, Igala, Igbo); Dafara or Latutuwa (Hausa); Agara or Orogbolo (Yoruba).

DISAGREEMENT, not reconciled: the hot-water soak is 15 minutes (Nigeria Galleria) against 8 to 10 minutes (Odoh). Both then squeeze. The two sources also default to different proteins — beef here, bushmeat or grasscutter in Odoh — and Odoh gives the egusi-ball component its Idoma name, abahi, which this source does not.

THE TECHNIQUE IS GENUINELY UNIQUE: stripping the inner bark of a stalk, beating it with a pestle, and squeezing out a mucilaginous sap as the thickener has no parallel in any other dish in this collection. It is the single most unusual preparation documented here.

A LEAD THAT FAILED: Idoma Voice Newspaper, a named Nigerian regional paper, carried a step-by-step okoho method at idomavoice.com but the fetch failed on a robots.txt timeout. It remains the best outstanding lead for this dish.

GAP: the Middle Belt record is otherwise close to empty. Searches for GENDE, AKPU-AKPU and ISHWA (termites) each returned ZERO results. RUAM NAHAR or RUAM KUMEN, Tiv pounded yam, has exactly one dedicated source — mytivfoodrecipes.blogspot.com — which is stuck in an HTTPS-to-HTTP redirect loop that could not be resolved, so no Tiv recipe is published in this collection at all. The blog also calls the dish 'Ruam Kumen' rather than 'ruam nahar', and which qualifier is correct could not be verified.
storage: 3 days refrigerated. The sap's thickening slackens on reheating.
reheating: Very low heat. Do not boil.
healthBenefits: The okoho sap is a soluble mucilaginous fibre.
Melon seed supplies protein, magnesium and zinc.
Two varieties of fermented locust bean give B vitamins and glutamates.
culturalNote: Okoho belongs to the Idoma of Benue State and it is Christmas and village-celebration food. The technique — a thickener wrung by hand out of plant bark — has no counterpart in the rest of Nigerian cooking, where thickeners come from seeds, tubers and flours. It is the kind of preparation that survives because nothing else does the same job.
